analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in Augusto against immigration service. Mr. Bixby, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. This case is here on certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. A divided panel of that court affirmed a final administrative decision of the Board of Immigration Appeals, finding that the petitioner in this case is an alien and that he is deportable from the United States. The petitioner claims to be a citizen of the United States and that he was born here in 1924. When he was two and a half years of age, his mother sent him to Italy to live with her sister and brother-in-law. Now, these facts are somewhat in dispute, are they not? They are in dispute. This is the petitioner's version of the facts, Your Honor. That's correct. Are his versions, is there some variety in his versions of the facts? There's some inconsistency in the record, Your Honor. Yes, there is. The administrative hearings were held over the course of several years in time, and as far as dates are concerned, there are inconsistent dates as to when he claims birth in the United States. There are inconsistencies, as you call them, in terms of what kind of documents were submitted by the petitioner? Yes, the only document that was submitted by the petitioner consisted of a birth certificate, Your Honor. This was a birth certificate that showed the petitioner to be born in the year of 1921. We take the position because of evidence that was testimony that was later produced in the administrative hearings and because of certain developments that the petitioner was not, in fact, born in the year of 1921, that the birth certificate is not a birth certificate that relates to the petitioner's birth, that, in fact, the petitioner was born in the year of 1924. How did the, I have some recollection that the hearing examiner characterized this document as fraudulent or something in that way? Is that correct? I don't think that's correct, Your Honor. I don't recall. Or some such thing? I don't recall anything in the record as far as the hearing, the immigration judge, the hearing officer in the administrative proceedings, saying that the document was fraudulent. He did find that the document did not belong to the petitioner, did not reflect the petitioner's birth. So that he was presenting a birth certificate that belonged to somebody else. Yes. I suppose that's where the illusion, the pejorative term came somewhere in the record. Yes, Your Honor, I believe so. So the petitioner contends, well, the petitioner's evidence tends to establish that he lived in Italy until the year of 1951 and that he then returned to the United States. The sister and brother-in-law, the petitioner's mother, affiliated him in Italy. He lived with them until his return here in the year of 1951. His primary proof in the administrative proceedings as far as birth in the United States is concerned, consisted of the testimony of these two people who he lived with and who affiliated him in Italy and the testimony of his half-brother who was born and lives here in the United States. The government's case rests on documents that were submitted in the administrative proceedings that purport to show that the petitioner was born in Italy in the year of 1927. As far as the testimony of the petitioner's witnesses was concerned, the immigration judge that conducted the deportation hearings rejected this testimony as being not credible. He found that the petitioner was born in Italy and that he was an alien deportable in order that he be deported to Italy. The Board of Immigration Appeals deferred to the immigration judge on the question of credibility and affirmed his decision. In the Board's decision, there is a statement, which is a very important statement, I think, and that is that if believed, the petitioner's witnesses, the testimony of the petitioner's witnesses, clearly refutes the otherwise strong documentary case made by the government as to alienage. The decision of the Board of Immigration Appeals was taken by petition for review to the Ninth Circuit. In the petition for review, the Ninth Circuit was requested to transfer the proceedings under Section 106A.5 of the Immigration and Nationality Act to a district court for a hearing de novo on the question of citizenship. The Ninth Circuit declined to do this on the ground that the petitioner had not presented a colorable claim to U.S. citizenship in his administrative proceedings. Now, the question that's presented by this case is a question that has not yet, has never heretofore been considered by this court, and that is the proper interpretation of Section 106A.5 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. This is part of a large section, Section 106, that was enacted in 1961 that is a substantial revision of the procedures for obtaining judicial review of a final administrative order of deportation. The key feature of Section 106 is to eliminate district courts from the judicial review of deportation orders and to require that an alien go directly into a court of appeals, file a petition for review, and that the court of appeals has exclusive jurisdiction to determine the validity of a final order of deportation on the administrative record. The one exception, of course, to that is the section that's involved in this case, and that is 106A.5, which provides that where a person has presented a claim to citizenship, and that claim is not a frivolous claim, and there is a genuine issue of material fact, the court of appeals must transfer the proceedings to the U.S. District Court for the residents of the petitioner, and a trial de novo is had in that district court to determine the question of citizenship. This exception is necessary because of this court's decisions going back to Ng Fung Ho v. White, where it was held that any resident of the United States who claims to be a citizen has a constitutional right to a judicial trial on that claim if his evidence presented in the administrative proceedings is sufficient, if believed, to support a finding of citizenship. The initial question in this case, I think, is whether Congress intended to change the evidentiary standard when it enacted Section 106A.5. The case law prior to 1961 had been that the test for obtaining judicial determination of citizenship was the substantial evidence test. Now, there's no legislative history one way or the other on the subject of whether Congress intended to make any change in the burden of proof. But the fact that the Congress did employ summary judgment language in 106A.5 strongly suggests, I think, that they did intend to relax the burden of proof, that something less than substantial evidence was intended to be required to obtain judicial determination of nationality. Mr. Bixby, do you think that the word frivolous is an additional qualification to a genuine issue of material fact? I'm not sure that it is. I think that if there's a genuine issue of material fact, it's quite hard to perceive of any situation where there would be a frivolous claim and also a genuine, I mean, if it's a genuine issue of material fact, to me it can't be a frivolous claim. I think it's really redundant. And I don't think... By contrast, if it's frivolous, there is no genuine issue of material fact. Is that true? I think that would hold true, Your Honor. What relief are you asking for here? Simply that this be heard by the district court? Yes, Your Honor, that's all. Nothing else. Nothing else, Your Honor, no. In the administrative proceedings, there were various forms of discretionary relief from deportation that were applied for in the alternative, without, of course, waiving our claim to citizenship. And these forms of relief were not granted, but I don't believe they're at issue here because we did not argue in our briefs before the Ninth Circuit. We didn't make these points in the briefs, and we solely confined the briefs to the transfer issue. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit found that there was no colorable claim to citizenship. Do you view that as the equivalent of holding that the claim was frivolous? I think the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, and especially I say that for several reasons, the court cited a case that was decided prior to 1961, a case that dealt with, actually it was a case that only contained dictum. Kessler v. Strecker, Your Honor. Correct. Correct. And that was a case that did, in dictum, mention the substantial evidence rule. And I think the Court of Appeals, the majority of the Court of Appeals, found that the petitioner had not satisfied the substantial evidence rule. It didn't quite say that, though, did it? Well, I don't think it quite said that. I think the dissent points out, aside from that, well, the dissent points out that the correct function of the Court of Appeals is not to determine credibility, not to act as a fact-pinder. And I think that's what the majority of the Court of Appeals did in this case. Well, supposing that there were a birth certificate showing that a person claiming to be a national was, in fact, born in a town in Italy, and the claimant did not contest the birth certificate, and we would offer any explanation as to why it was not a perfectly valid document. I take it your client here does make some contest to that. But supposing that he didn't. And it was simply a question of this document versus the claimant's sworn statement that he was born in the United States. Now, would that be a non-frivolous claim? No, I think that would be a frivolous claim because I think the case that you put is really a bare assertion of citizenship without any evidentiary support at all. In other words, just a statement, even though made of first-hand knowledge, will not overcome an unchallenged document. That's correct. I don't think a person that merely asserts citizenship and that has no evidence to support it is entitled to transfer proceedings under this statute, Your Honor. How do you suppose the Court of Appeals came to think that the decisive question here was whether or not there was a colorable claim to United States nationality? The majority found there wasn't, and the dissenting judge thought that there was a colorable claim, and that phrase is nowhere to be found in the statute, is it? No, it isn't, John. Do you suppose they thought the issue was whether or not it was frivolous or whether or not there was a genuine issue of material fact? Because those are the two statutory tests. That's correct. I think, again, and it's impossible to say for certain because it's a very brief decision. But each of them, both the Court and the dissent, speak as though the issue were whether or not there was a colorable claim, and that particular test is nowhere in the statute, is it? That's true. There's two statutory tests of whether or not it's frivolous and whether or not there's a genuine issue of material fact. To which issue do you suppose the Court of Appeals was directing its attention, or to both? Well, again, I'm not certain that these are two separate requirements. I think that really there is a redundancy here, that frivolous and genuine issue of material fact, if it's a non-frivolous claim, I think that there's a genuine issue of material fact and vice versa. And you think colorable claim is a suitable synonym for both of the statutory phrases? It wouldn't probably have been the phrase that I would have used, but I think that the majority, well, the majority and the dissent, as you point out, both use that phrase, and I think they must have thought that it was... But the majority cited that Kessler case, which used the... Substantial evidence. Substantial evidence under the old statute. And it did say it also, the short majority opinion went on in the last sentence, saying it also does not, the evidence does not meet the standards set forth in Kessler v. Strecker, which wasn't substantial. Nor does it meet, as though that were an additional... As though that were an additional requirement of the statute. Correct. Correct. I believe that the case, well, to begin with, I should say there, as the court realizes, I'm sure, there are merely a handful of decisions from the Court of Appeals, reported decisions, that have construed Section 106A5. And in looking at these decisions, I think that the case of Pignatello v. Attorney General is the only decision that really deals in any depth with the statute. Now, in that case, the court viewed the statute as being essentially a summary judgment statute. And it did state that as far as the standard that must be satisfied, the statute, the statute only requires a modicum of substantiality to the claim of citizenship and that the claim not be a frivolous one. The court obviously, although it didn't expressly state this, it obviously felt that there was some change in the evidentiary standard from substantial evidence over to a modicum of substantiality. And I would suppose that the fact that the statute employs the summary judgment language is the basis for the Second Circuit's conclusion that only a modicum of substantiality is required. The case of Pignatello also points out that the function of the Court of Appeals is not to determine credibility of evidence, and it's not to sift and to weigh the evidence. But that's the function of the district court. If the proceedings are transferred to the district court, the district court acting as the trier of fact has that function. In the first instance, it's the function of the hearing examiner, is it not? If there is, well, in the first instance, you're correct, Your Honor. Administratively, it's the hearing examiner who makes this decision initially, and then the Board of Immigration appeals the final administrative authority. And what do you say the hearing examiner concluded about the... He decided, Your Honor, that the testimony of the petitioner's witness in this case was not credible. He did not accept their testimony as being truthful, and therefore he rejected the testimony. And this is why you wanted a novo hearing. This is exactly it. We feel that we're entitled to a judicial determination, and we feel that this case turned on the issue of credibility. And where that's the case... But must the district court try every such case, deportation ultimately, if credibility is an issue? Not at all, Your Honor. It's limited to only this case. Not only does the Constitution require, in a case where a person claims citizenship, that the district court, where there is, as we say, a modicum of substantiality, as the court in Pignatello said, a modicum of substantiality to that claim, it's for the district court to judicially determine that claim. But in no other case involving deportation, Your Honor, would the district court be involved at all. Section 106 makes it very clear that courts of appeals determine the validity of final orders of deportation on the administrative record in all cases except for cases where there is a claim to citizenship made. But you would say, I take it, that administrative resolutions of credibility in cases like this, where there's a claim to citizenship, if you believe the person, if you believe one side, the fellow's a citizen, and if you disbelieve him, he isn't. You take it, those situations would always have to go to the district court. Always, Your Honor. I think so, because it's a credibility issue, and that was what this section was designed to, well, designed to codify, actually, the constitutional right, the Fifth Amendment due process right. And you confine that to cases where the issue is citizenship. That's exactly correct. Or not citizenship. Exactly correct, Your Honor, yes. May I give you an example of the point that Mr. Justice White just put to you? Let's assume in this case that you had documentary records such as those that were presented that showed on that face that the plaintiff was born in Italy, was married in Italy, assumed, fellow, there were no other documentary records of any kind, and the only other evidence was the plaintiff took the stand and said those documents are false. Well, I'll add one other set of facts to it. You had an individual who had a long criminal record, as this individual had. Does all one have to do is to stand up and swear that he's an American citizen without presenting any supporting evidence of any kind except his own statement? Well, I think you have to present more than your own statement. But I believe that there would have to be more evidence than that, certainly. Well, what if he said, he not only made the bald assertion which you before said wasn't enough, what if he said, I was born on such and such a date in Detroit, Michigan, and my parents were so-and-so, and he attempted to support his claim of citizenship by some facts? Now, if he called somebody else, like he did here, and they said, yes, we know we've known this man in our life, and he was born in Detroit, Michigan, we knew him as a child, and he was here, you would say at least in that latter case it would require a retrial in the district court. Well, I think in the latter case you would have a... What about the former, where he just himself attempts to support his claim with his own assertion? I don't think there would be a modicum of substantiality of the claim in the former case. Yet under the summary judgment rule, the interested party himself, by denying or asserting, can survive a motion for summary judgment. So if you concede that, you admit this isn't the same as the summary judgment rule. I think this is essentially a summary judgment statute, and I think the courts of appeals that have dealt with this statute have treated it as such. Well, but then your answer to Justice White's question should be that it only should take the statement of the affiant under oath that I am a citizen of the United States born in Detroit without any supporting witness at all, because that's the uniformly applied summary judgment test, as I understand. Well, all I can say on that, certainly if that's the test, if it truly were a summary judgment statute, then perhaps that's so. Well, I'm questioning you. Yes. You know, I'm not purporting to give an answer. I think that the cases that have been decided by the courts of appeals have not viewed the statute as strictly summary judgment. That is, they've required that there be something more than a sworn statement by the petitioner to the effect that I am a U.S. citizen. So you think there can be an administrative determination of the alien or the supposed alien's own credibility, but there can't be administrative rejection of the credibility of any witnesses he calls? If he would win if their testimony was believed. Well, I think that there has, again, I suppose I'm coming back to this modicum of substantiality. I think there has to be something more than... Well, I guess you say at least if he calls some other witnesses and they present some testimony, you're entitled to a trial in the district court. Well, I think it would probably be... You would have to look at the testimony of the witnesses that he called also. As to what they could testify to, their testimony might be worthless. At least that isn't your case. That isn't my case. I think the closest case to that is the Rossano case, which is in some sight of the person. Mr. Dick, what do you do with these three alleged convictions? I don't think they have any bearing on whether the man is a citizen of the United States or not. They might have a bearing on his credibility, though, because all the convictions were for fraud or something. Well, two of them were in Italy and one was in Alaska. That's correct. Shows you quite a traveler. Yes, it does, Your Honor. But you don't feel any obligation to explain them at all? I don't feel any obligation to explain them. Maybe that explains why the court took place to do that. Well, I'm relying more on the testimony of the witnesses called by the petitioner than I am on petitioner's testimony. Are those the witnesses? The witnesses were... The examiner said he did not believe that they were not credible? That's correct, Your Honor. They were in a position, though, that the Pianettis, who were the couple in Italy that affiliated with the petitioner, with whom he lived, they were in the best position to know the facts as far as his birth. Of course, he was only two and a half years of age when he was sent to Italy, and he wouldn't know these things, but they would, and they were in the best position to know, and so I'm relying more on their testimony than I would upon the petitioner's testimony. And you think you're entitled to have a district judge, nothing less than a district judge, make the evaluation of the credibility of the witnesses? I think we're entitled to a trial de novo by a district judge who would observe the demeanor of the witnesses and who would determine their credibility. That doesn't give much utility to the function of the hearing examiners, does it? In a particular case where U.S. citizenship is involved, Your Honor, it doesn't leave the hearing officer as the final authority. Well, can you imagine any case where the claim of citizenship could not be made? I think it must be very rarely made, Your Honor, considering the fact that there is only a handful of cases since 1961 that have been decided. My question was, can you imagine a case where it could not be made? Oh, I suppose it could be made in any case that came before the immigration authorities, Your Honor. Up to now, it has been apparently thought that the determination of the hearing examiner was sufficient. Not at all, Your Honor, not by the courts of appeals. The courts of appeals have... You're talking about the administrative, the reviewing immigration, what do you call that, the Board of Immigration Appeals? Board of Immigration Appeals, Your Honor. It hasn't... I'm not quite certain I understand your question, but I understand it properly. Within the administrative framework, it has been... Credence has been given to the credibility findings of the hearing examiner. That's correct, within the administrative framework, yes. Yes. When was Section 106A5 enacted? 1961, Your Honor. 61. Yes. Yes. Mr. Bixby, just so I have it clearly in mind, the evidence that's consistent with your client's present version of events is that of the witnesses, the two Pianettis, his adoptive parents... Yes. ...and his half-brother, Carmen Ripolino... That's correct, Your Honor. ...and then his own testimony. Now, is there any documentary testimony whatsoever that corroborates any portion of their testimony? In the administrative record, there is no document to corroborate this testimony. That's correct. But your claim, as I understand it, is that if we were to believe the testimony... I mean, if the trier of fact were to believe the testimony of those three persons, they would establish citizenship. Yes, that was the conclusion, Your Honor, of the Board of Immigration Appeals. They said the same thing. Yes. Yes. May I ask you a question about congressional content, intent? I realize, of course, you are relying on the words of the statute, but here we have a case in which the immigration judge found, and I'm reading from the record, that the claim to citizenship here has been knowingly false from its inception. Knowingly false. All the way down the roadway. I thought it was something else. He's had two or three hearings before an immigration judge and a couple before the board. The board affirmed that conclusion of totally false testimony all the way. The Court of Appeals reviewed it and concluded there was no colorable claim to citizenship. And now you're asking us to start all over again at the level of the district court, then come back up to the Court of Appeals, presumably. Do you think Congress could have intended a regime of litigation of that character? I think that Congress intended the words of 106A5 make it quite clear that Congress intended that when a case, when it's citizenship, U.S. citizenship that's involved, and the administrative findings, findings by the hearing officer and Board of Immigration Appeals, turn on the issue of credibility, that certainly that man is entitled. It didn't use the word credibility. It spoke of a frivolous claim. Well, I think it's quite clear that the Board of Immigration Appeals felt that the determination on the issue of citizenship was one that turned on the issue of credibility. They deferred to the immigration judge as the trier of fact as far as the issue of credibility was concerned. So I think that the statute was certainly designed to give the individual who claims to be a citizen and who has presented a modicum, anyway, of substantiality to this claim, to give him that right to have a judicial determination made. That, of course, has been decided by this Court that that is a constitutional right, that that's going back to Ng Fung Ho v. White. Well, just offhand, I can't recall any other system of review in the federal system quite comparable to the position you are taking. I recognize you have a statute with special language, and I would make the argument you're arguing. I'm just wondering whether Congress conceivably could have had any such intention. I think they had to have that intention, Your Honor, because the man has a constitutional right, and they had to make an exception in this section, Section 106, and give him that constitutional right of a judicial trial of the issue of citizenship if he does present in his administrative hearing evidence that at least has a modicum of substantiality. And if this is a unique procedure, it's because deportation is a unique process, i.e., it's a monstrously unconstitutional thing to forcibly deport a citizen to some foreign land. I think that's correct, Your Honor. Thank you. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, Petitioner is seeking a hearing de novo in the United States District Court of his claim that he is a United States citizen by virtue of his birth in the United States. We contend that Petitioner's claim of citizenship is frivolous and that he has not raised a genuine issue of material fact concerning his claim of U.S. citizenship. Therefore, the Court of Appeals properly held Petitioner deportable on the basis of the administrative record before it without referring the proceedings to the District Court for a hearing. Section 106A5 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which Petitioner asserts requires de novo trial in his case, is part of a general revision of provisions for judicial review of deportation orders. This revision, which was enacted in 1961, was, as Petitioner's Council has noted, intended to prevent repetitious litigation of deportation order cases. Mrs. Judson, it would help me if you went a little, if you raised your voice a little bit, went a little slower. The revision prevented this repetitious litigation by eliminating district court review in most cases. Indeed, the Court of Appeals generally review deportation order cases on the administrative record. Section 106A5 is a narrow exception to this scheme. It provides a de novo hearing in the District Court when a person subject to final deportation order makes a substantial claim of citizenship. But in keeping with the general purposes of Section 106A5, not every claim of United States citizenship need be referred to the District Court for trial. Instead, the section requires the person requesting transfer to make a showing that his claim is not frivolous and to show that there's a genuine issue of material fact as to that person's nationality. Only if these two showings are made must the Court of Appeals transfer the case to the District Court. As Petitioner... I'm just going to ask if you would state your view as to what the difference is between frivolous and the existence or absence of a material issue of fact. The statute isn't entirely clear as to whether those are two different standards. In part, they use the term genuine issue of material fact to distinguish those non-frivolous cases where there's an issue of fact from those non-frivolous cases where there's an issue of law. Those cases where there's an issue of law that is non-frivolous can be determined by the Court of Appeals under the statute. And the non-frivolous cases where there's an issue of fact, a genuine issue of material fact, are intended to be referred to the District Court. The frivolous claim can be disposed of by the Court of Appeals under the language of the statute merely by the holding that the claim is frivolous. Like they did here, right? They appear to have done here, yes. Can do that on a factual issue as well as an issue of law? Yes. Under the way the statute is written, a frivolous claim of an issue of law could be disposed of under the frivolous standard as well. Another puzzling aspect of this statute to me, and perhaps you can answer it, it refers to the pleadings and affidavits filed by the parties. Are we limited to those in reviewing the record in this case? In this case, the pleadings incorporated the entire administrative record. Including all the testimony of witnesses? Yes, that was all before the Court of Appeals and was referred to in the pleadings. Presumably that was intended to be picked up by the term pleadings. Again, as you note, the statute isn't entirely clear, but that had to be, I would assume, was the intention of the Congress. And there's no issue in the case on that? No. Oh, excuse me, Your Honor. There is an issue in the case as to what record, what part of the record the Court of Appeals was permitted to look to in passing on whether there was a genuine issue of material fact. A petitioner contends that the Court of Appeals was not permitted to go beyond reading the opinion of the Board of Immigration Examiners. And we contend that the plain language of the statute permits the Court of Appeals to look at the pleadings, including the administrative record incorporated in the pleadings, as well as any affidavits that are provided to the Court of Appeals. And we have to read it all without any help from the Court of Appeals. Is there any way we can do it without reading all of it? There are fairly good summaries in the various opinions of the immigration judges. Well, what would we do on our job if we did? Those are merely a starting point, Your Honor. And then we'd have to read the whole thing. You think that's what Congress meant, the dumping all the air? Do you think Congress meant that? I believe that Congress intended that these cases, which are factual cases, would normally end in the Court of Appeals. What evidence did the government put in, other than what? The service presented a comprehensive documentary case in the administrative hearings. These began with records of birth of Petitioner, three separate independently created recorded records showing his birth in Italy in 1927 as a foundling who was recorded under the name Vincenzo Di Paoli. What live testimony was that? The government did not present any live testimony to my recollection. But the defendant did. Yes, the defendant did. And the Court of Appeals just brushed that aside. Sworn testimony. The Court of Appeals had the entire record before it. Well, the Court of Appeals failed to mention anything about it. That's correct, Your Honor. The Court of Appeals merely stated in conclusory terms that there had been no callable claims. So the Court of Appeals had the choice of sending this to be decided on its facts to the district court or to us, so they sent it to us. Mrs. Jenton, before you get back into your argument, if we disregard the Petitioner's own testimony entirely because he was impeached repeatedly, and if we merely assume for purposes of decision that it's at least theoretically possible that the trier of fact might believe the Pianettis, who, as I understand it, were the couple that adopted him or affiliated him, according to his version, and the testimony of his brother-in-law, would you agree that if that testimony were believed that he made a non-frivolous claim of citizenship? Our contention is that the Pianetti's testimony and that of his brother-in-law cannot be read in isolation, that when their testimony is read against the rest of the record, including Petitioner's own testimony on a variety of occasions, that the result is that the Pianettis have not... not told the truth. But my question is, if we were to assume that the trier of fact thought they told the truth, and you accepted that for the purposes of my question, would you then agree that he has made a non-frivolous claim of citizenship? Assuming that what the Pianetti said was true, which is that the documents which the service has provided in the record... were prepared by his grandfather in order to hide the fact that he was illegitimate and so forth. If that is the case, then... And if none of the previous testimony were in the record or was disregarded, then Petitioner, probably that would have been the absolute minimum showing to get to the district court. However...
